comparison: Both strongly support the main finding that different computational models best fit CON (M1) and BPD (M4) groups. OpenEval emphasizes model comparison statistics (exceedance probabilities) and model recovery validation (C36-C39, C124-C125), while peer reviewers describe this as the 'main finding' with 'convincing' evidence and 'an important step towards better understanding cognitive processes in BPD.'

Both support the confirmation of pre-registered hypotheses. OpenEval explicitly evaluates claims C3-C4, C17-C18, C72-C73 about hypothesis confirmation, while peer reviewers affirm the main finding without specifically addressing the pre-registration aspect. Substantial overlap in claims (C3, C4, C17, C18, C36-C39, C72, C73) indicates alignment on the core model comparison results.

Both support equivalent behavioral performance between groups despite different computational mechanisms. OpenEval emphasizes statistical tests and model predictions (C29-C31, C100, C126-C127), while peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings through their statement that evidence is 'convincing' and the task design is 'sophisticated and novel.'

Perfect claim overlap (C52-C54, C57, C74, C101). Both support the trial-by-trial Kullback-Leibler divergence analysis showing differential updating for relative vs. absolute reward. OpenEval provides detailed statistical evidence, while peer reviewers implicitly accept through statements about 'thorough investigation' using 'mechanistic computational models.'

Strong alignment on social contagion and belief shift findings (C58-C63, C95). OpenEval provides detailed statistical evidence from models M1 and M3, while peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the 'clever and sophisticated' computational methods. Minor difference: peer review includes C82 which OpenEval addresses separately in R14.

Both support the exploratory network analysis linking childhood trauma, mentalizing, and belief parameters (C64, C67, C76-C77). OpenEval notes statistical evidence with FDR correction and acknowledges some effects diminished when controlling for group. Peer reviewers explicitly appreciate that authors 'clearly label exploratory analyses where applicable.'

Perfect claim overlap (C19-C25). Both support the sample characterization and group matching. OpenEval provides detailed evidence from Table 1 showing appropriate matching on demographics and expected differences on clinical measures. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through statements about 'convincing' evidence and 'sophisticated task design.'

Perfect claim overlap (C26-C28, C33-C35). Both support the behavioral choice patterns showing group differences only for prosocial vs individualistic choices. OpenEval provides specific statistical tests across phases, while peer reviewers implicitly accept through statements about 'convincing' evidence and 'novel task design.'

Strong alignment on reaction time and temporal dynamics (C80, C134-C136). OpenEval provides detailed statistical evidence showing time effects and lack of group differences. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through statements about 'clever and sophisticated' methods and 'thorough investigation.' OpenEval also includes C31-C32 which peer review addresses in R8.

Both support the interpretation that BPD participants maintain neutral priors and separate absolute/relative reward representations. OpenEval focuses on model properties (C43-C44) and parameter evidence (C89-C90), while peer reviewers accept the mechanistic interpretations (C89-C93, C102, C116) as 'an important step towards better understanding cognitive processes in BPD.'

Perfect claim overlap on BPD mechanistic interpretation (C89-C93). Both support the integration of current findings with prior BPD literature. OpenEval notes the interpretation about 'splitting' is somewhat speculative, while peer reviewers accept the mechanistic account as contributing to understanding cognitive processes in BPD.

Both support the model validation procedures. OpenEval emphasizes excellent model and parameter recovery statistics (C128, C130, C132) and correlations with behavioral choices. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the 'clever and sophisticated' computational methods and acknowledge the 'thorough investigation,' accepting the validation analyses (C124-C128).

Both support the theoretical integration with prior literature. OpenEval evaluates claims about self-insertion effects, social contagion, and impression formation (C78-C85), while peer reviewers note 'connections to the theoretical framework are presented with much greater clarity' and findings have 'theoretical or practical implications beyond a single subfield' (C78-C79, C81, C83-C85, C108-C110, C112).

Both support the theoretical and methodological contributions. OpenEval evaluates the integration of Bayesian inference with social value orientation (C108-C112), while peer reviewers accept the theoretical contributions and note the paradigm is 'potentially relevant for the investigation of other psychiatric conditions.'

Divergent evaluations of clinical implications. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting C104 contradicts model comparison results and C105-C107 are speculative requiring empirical validation. Peer reviewers SUPPORT these claims, stating findings are 'important and intriguing, with theoretical or practical implications' and the paradigm is 'potentially relevant for other psychiatric conditions.'

Both support the acknowledged limitations. OpenEval evaluates claims about alternative explanations for neutral priors (C113-C116), while peer reviewers accept the transparent discussion of limitations and scope (C113-C115, C118), noting the manuscript 'is much clearer and easier to follow now.'

Both support the discussion of study scope and generalization limitations. OpenEval evaluates the strength of observation-only design (C117) and appropriate acknowledgment that naturalistic generalization requires testing (C118). Peer reviewers accept the authors' transparent discussion of scope.

Both support the methodological validation. OpenEval evaluates the matching algorithm success (C32) as critical for interpreting learning results. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through statements about 'convincing' evidence, though they focus more broadly on sample characteristics.

Both support the integration with neuroimaging literature and mechanistic interpretation. OpenEval evaluates claims about blunted neural responses in BPD (C96-C99) and network analysis evidence. Peer reviewers accept the exploratory findings (C98) as appropriately labeled and part of the thorough investigation.

Both support the interpretation accounting for alternative explanations. OpenEval evaluates the discussion of M4 vs M1 for BPD (C102-C103) as appropriately identifying future research directions. Peer reviewers accept this mechanistic interpretation as contributing to understanding BPD cognitive processes.

Both support the model simplicity justification. OpenEval evaluates the design choice to use a simple model (C119-C120) as reasonable given excellent recovery results. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through praise of 'clever and sophisticated' computational methods and validation procedures.

Both support the balanced assessment of contributions and limitations. OpenEval evaluates future research directions and methodological strengths (C121-C123). Peer reviewers accept the clinical relevance (C121) and note the paradigm's potential for investigating other psychiatric conditions.

Both support the theoretical framing and background. OpenEval evaluates the literature-supported rationale (C1-C2, C7-C16). Peer reviewers note the 'connections to the theoretical framework are presented with much greater clarity,' accepting the background claims as well-documented.

Both support the summary findings. OpenEval evaluates C5 (reduced belief updating in BPD) as supported by behavioral and computational evidence, and C6 (trauma associations) as supported by network analysis. Peer reviewers implicitly accept C5 through their statement about 'convincing' evidence for the main findings.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the exploratory correlation between relative reward preferences and harmful intent attributions (C71), noting it requires replication and more direct mechanistic testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; peer reviewers generally accepted exploratory analyses when clearly labeled but did not specifically address this claim.
